rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (2026) 112 Article Number: 108465. Date of Publication: 1 Feb 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Accurate but efficient retinal vessel segmentation is crucial for clinical diagnosis. Although current deep learning-based methods have achieved satisfactory segmentation performance, there are still some challenges, such as the lack of microvessels and insufficient global modelling. To address these problems, we propose a Dual-Decoder Progressive Fusion Network (D(2)PF-Net). First, a multi-scale vessel enhancement (MVE) module is devised to alleviate the lack of microvessels. Second, a decoding feature fusion (DFF) module is embedded into the left branch of D(2)PF-Net to progressively enrich the decoder with sufficient global contextual information. Simultaneously, a cross-scale context fusion (CCF) module is inserted into the right branch of D(2)PF-Net to make the encoder focus more on multi-scale pathological information. Finally, a multi-scale feature aggregation (MFA) module is designed to aggregate complementary multi-scale semantics information from different branches. Extensive experiments have been conducted on five retinal vessel and two polyp image datasets, validating the efficiency and generalization ability of D(2)PF-Net, which is quite competitive compared to the state-of-the-art methods. More importantly, D(2)PF-Net is relatively lightweight, efficient and interpretable for real-time prediction, further promoting its practicality.

rows.TITLE: TITLE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: DGSSA: Domain generalization with structural and stylistic augmentation for retinal vessel segmentation

rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Neural Networks (2026) 194 Article Number: 108118. Date of Publication: 1 Feb 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Retinal vascular morphology plays a crucial role in diagnosing diseases such as diabetes, glaucoma, and hypertension, making accurate segmentation of retinal vessels essential for early intervention. Traditional segmentation methods assume that training and testing data share similar distributions, which can lead to poor performance on unseen domains due to domain shifts caused by variations in imaging devices and patient demographics. This paper presents a novel approach, DGSSA, for retinal vessel image segmentation that enhances model generalization by combining structural and stylistic augmentation strategies. We utilize a space colonization algorithm to generate diverse vascular-like structures that closely mimic actual retinal vessels, which are then used to generate pseudo-retinal images with an improved Pix2Pix model, allowing the segmentation model to learn a broader range of structure distributions. Additionally, we utilize PixMix to apply random photometric augmentations and introduce uncertainty perturbations, enriching the stylistic diversity of fundus images and further improving the model's robustness and generalization across varying imaging conditions. Our framework, which employs a DeepLabv3+ model with a MobileNetV2 backbone as its segmentation network, has been rigorously evaluated on four challenging datasets—DRIVE, CHASEDB1, HRF, and STARE—achieving Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 78.45%, 78.62%, 72.66% and 82.17%, respectively, with an average DSC of 77.98%. These results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches, validating its effectiveness and highlighting its potential for clinical application in automated retinal vessel analysis.

rows.TITLE: TITLE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Improvement of an eye disease detection model by using the denoising diffusion implicit model

rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Computational Biology and Chemistry (2026) 120 Article Number: 108677. Date of Publication: 1 Feb 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: With rapid developments in artificial intelligence (AI), the discussion about and applications of generative AI have increased substantially. Generative AI has extensive and valuable applications in many industrial and medical fields and is a possible solution for industries that struggle to collect large quantities of data. The present study evaluated the use of generative AI in eye disease prediction. Because retinal images are difficult to acquire, this study used a generative AI model [i.e., the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM)] to conduct data augmentation, thereby improving the accuracy of a convolutional neural network (CNN) model developed for eye disease detection. This study adopted the DDIM primarily for its high inference speed and ability to consistently generate high-quality samples in a limited number of steps, making it suitable for tasks that require high-quality medical images. With the increasing prevalence of electronic products, the number of patients with retinopathy or optic neuropathy is increasing annually, and patients are experiencing these diseases at increasingly younger ages. Moreover, eye diseases such as glaucoma and macular degeneration are becoming increasingly common in modern society. The developed CNN model exhibited a 3 % higher accuracy when it was trained using the data generated by the DDIM than when it was trained without these data. This CNN model can screen eye disease symptoms early to enable patients to receive timely treatment, thereby mitigating the risk and consequences of eye diseases. The results of this study indicate that the training data generated using the DDIM can enhance the accuracy of early eye disease detection.

rows.TITLE: TITLE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Validation of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Anterior Chamber Depth Estimation Using a Smartphone-Compatible Slit Lamp Device

rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Ophthalmology Science (2026) 6:1 Article Number: 100906. Date of Publication: 1 Jan 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Purpose: Accurate evaluation of anterior chamber depth (ACD), a major risk factor for angle closure, is clinically important. Although standard techniques provide reliable measurements, they are often labor-intensive, technically demanding, and time-consuming. To address this, we previously developed an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm capable of estimating ACD from slit lamp photographs. This study sought to assess the performance of this AI model when applied via the Smart Eye Camera (SEC), a smartphone-compatible slit lamp imaging system, by comparing its estimates to those obtained with anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT) at a separate institution. Design: An evaluation of diagnostic test. Participants: Five hundred fifty-six phakic eyes (268 nondilated and 288 dilated eyes) from 329 Asian patients. Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed on images captured using both the SEC and AS-OCT. Anterior chamber depth values generated by the AI model embedded in the SEC were compared with corresponding measurements obtained using AS-OCT. Main Outcome Measures: Metrics, including mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), Pearson correlation coefficient, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), were calculated to evaluate model performance. Results: The AI algorithm integrated into the SEC demonstrated the capability to estimate the ACD with an MAE of 0.119 ± 0.0949 mm and an MSE of 0.0233 ± 0.0557 mm. A strong correlation was observed between ACD measurements obtained using AS-OCT and those estimated by AI (R = 0.922; 95% confidence interval, 0.908–0.933). The ICC for agreement between AI-estimated and AS-OCT-measured ACD was 0.903, indicating excellent reliability. Conclusions: Our AI model, embedded within the SEC platform, demonstrated high accuracy in estimating ACD when benchmarked against AS-OCT. Given its portability and user-friendliness, the SEC presents a promising option for accessible ACD screening across diverse clinical environments. Financial Disclosure(s): Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found in the Footnotes and Disclosures at the end of this article.

rows.TITLE: TITLE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Long-term stabilized iris tracking with unsupervised constraints on dynamic AS-OCT

rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Medical Image Analysis (2026) 107 Article Number: 103787. Date of Publication: 1 Jan 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) is responsible for half of all glaucoma-related blindness worldwide. The devastating disease is often clinically silent before causing irreversible visual damage. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy is the major diagnostic criterion for glaucoma. Patients with severe PACG have been clinically found to have significantly lower pupillary reflex velocity and higher iris rigidity. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) enables dynamic visualization of the ocular iris anatomy which cannot otherwise be acquired by other imaging modalities. However, automatic quantification of dynamic iris motion on AS-OCT has not yet been implemented. The main challenges lie in the frequent jitter of high-resolution optical imaging, irregular temporal variations of elastic features, and relatively scarce datasets. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised constraint-based jitter refinement tracking (CJRTrack) framework for long-term AS-OCT video tracking. CJRTrack primarily consists of three modules: it first extracts a set of key regions from low-resolution images using an off-the-shelf point tracking algorithm. Given the initialized frames and points, an unsupervised multi-frame differentiable registration network estimates the localized deformation field patch for corresponding high-resolution images. It then refines these predictions using a temporal topology constraint-based module, which explicitly ensures overall trajectory stabilization and tracking. Multi-scale evaluations on two independent AS-OCT datasets demonstrate that CJRTrack significantly outperforms existing tracking models in both accuracy and stability. The clinical adaptivity of the model is further assessed on a glaucoma dataset containing 543 diseased eyes. Jitter-corrected quantification is extracted and used to classify neuropathic damage in primary angle closure patients.

rows.TITLE: TITLE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Can a Natural Image-Based Foundation Model Outperform a Retina-Specific Model in Detecting Ocular and Systemic Diseases?

rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Ophthalmology Science (2026) 6:1 Article Number: 100923. Date of Publication: 1 Jan 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Purpose: DINOv2 is a natural image-based foundation model (FM), pretrained exclusively on 142 million natural images from the LVD-142M data set. In contrast, RETFound is a retina-specific FM, pretrained on ∼3 million images, including natural images, color fundus photos, and OCT images (∼1 million each). Despite DINOv2's massive pretraining data set, its application in ophthalmology and relative performance to domain-specific FMs remain understudied. To address this gap, we conducted a head-to-head comparative evaluation between DINOv2 and RETFound models across a range of downstream ocular and systemic disease tasks. Design: Retrospective head-to-head evaluation. Subjects: Ocular disease detection tasks included diabetic retinopathy (DR), glaucoma, and multiclass eye diseases, whereas systemic disease incidence prediction focused on the 3-year incidence of heart failure, myocardial infarction, and ischemic stroke. Eight open-source data sets (APTOS-2019, IDRID, MESSIDOR2 for DR; PAPILA, Glaucoma Fundus for glaucoma; JSIEC, Retina, OCTID for multiclass eye diseases) and the Moorfields AlzEye data set (for systemic diseases) were used for fine-tuning and internal testing. External test sets included the same open-source data sets (cross-dataset validation) and the UK Biobank (for systemic diseases). Methods: We replicated the fine-tuning methodology from the original RETFound study on 3 DINOv2 models (large, base, small). All models were fine-tuned on the respective data sets and evaluated through internal and external testing. Main Outcome Measures: Area under the receiver operating characteristics curve and 2-sided t-tests were used to compare models' performances. Results: For ocular disease detection, DINOv2 models generally outperformed RETFound. For DR, DINOv2-Large achieved AUCs of 0.850 to 0.952, exceeding RETFound's 0.823 to 0.944 (all P ≤ 0.007). For multiclass eye diseases, DINOv2-large (AUC = 0.892, Retina data set) surpassed RETFound (AUC = 0.846, P < 0.001). For glaucoma, DINOv2-base (AUC = 0.958, Glaucoma Fundus) outperformed RETFound (AUC = 0.940, P < 0.001). Conversely, for systemic disease incidence prediction, RETFound achieved superior AUCs of 0.796 (heart failure), 0.732 (myocardial infarction), and 0.754 (ischemic stroke), outperforming DINOv2's best models' AUC (0.663–0.771, all P < 0.001). This trend persisted in external validation. Conclusions: Our findings reveal the merits of DINOv2 in ocular disease detection tasks, whereas RETFound demonstrates an edge in systemic disease incidence prediction. These findings showcase the distinct scenarios where general-purpose and domain-specific FMs excel, highlighting the importance of aligning FM selection with task-specific requirements to optimize clinical performance. Financial Disclosure(s): Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found in the Footnotes and Disclosures at the end of this article.

rows.title: Automated Detection of Glaucoma From Topographic Features of ONH in Fundus
rows.patient_selection_support: Case-control design from hospital eye clinics. Subjects with ONH anomalies, major tilt, advanced retinopathy, poor image quality excluded. Not representative of screening population.
rows.index_test_support: Fully automated cascade-forward neural network; features extracted computationally without human intervention. System output produced independently of reference standard.
rows.reference_standard_support: Consensus of 2 masked glaucoma specialists using comprehensive clinical exam (slit-lamp, IOP Goldmann, gonioscopy, VF HFA 24-2/10-2, OCT/HRT). Disagreement cases excluded.
rows.flow_timing_support: All 314 eyes in reference test set received both index test and reference standard. 13 subjects excluded (7 poor quality, 6 disagreement) - minor proportion (7.6%).
rows.analysis_data_handling_support: Glaucoma suspects merged with confirmed glaucoma for binary evaluation. Training labels based on majority consensus of 5 graders on images alone. Threshold optimized post-hoc.
rows.notes: Cross-site validation (trained Site-B Madurai, tested Site-A Coimbatore). AUC=0.792. Hospital-based South India population only.

rows.databases: PubMed, Medline, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and ClinicalKey
rows.inclusion_summary: 1)Open-angle glaucoma 2)presenting fndings on the performance of DL in distinguishing glaucoma from the normal population using automated analyses of fundus or OCT images
rows.exclusion_summary:
1) did not assess primary openangle glaucoma. Case reports, guidelines, conference papers, letters, editorials, and review articles 2)did not provide primary outcomes related to predicting glaucoma onset, detecting glaucoma progression, or distinguishing glaucoma from other ocular diseases 3)data insuffciency defined by absence of adequate information required to construct a 2 × 2 contingency
table for the testing result
rows.search_keywords: “Glaucoma”, “Open-angle glaucoma”, and “Glaucomatous optic neuropathy”—with the following keywords associated with artifcial intelligence: “Deep learning”, “Machine learning”, and “Artifcial intelligence”. Terms involving outcomes were also used, such as“Glaucoma diagnosis” and “Glaucoma Progression”. No language or time restrictions were applied.
rows.methods: 1.bivariate random-effects model 2.hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (sROC) curve plots 3. quantifed the variation of effect size due to inter-study heterogeneity with forest plots, 4. publication bias, Deeks’ funnel plots 5. Bonferroni correction to adjust for the increased risk of type I errors
rows.main_results: For fundus photography, the pooled sensitivity and specifcity were 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89–0.94) and 0.93 (95% CI: 0.90–0.95), respectively, with an AUROC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.88–0.92). For the OCT imaging, the pooled sensitivity and specifcity were 0.90 (95% CI: 0.84–0.94) and 0.87 (95% CI: 0.81–0.91), respectively, with an AUROC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.83–0.90).
rows.data_extraction_focus: first author’s name, publication year, country of origin, type of images (fundus or OCT), primary DL classifer, total size of image data, data sources for training and validation, total size of testing data, ground truth information, validation type (internal or external), as well as the sensitivity, specifcity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve of the most effective DL algorithm outcomes obtained from each validation or testing dataset
rows.limitations: 1) not integrating functional assessment data, such as VF measurements for glaucoma progression 2) heterogeneity among the included and analyzed studies. Variations in DL architectures, imaging protocols, and patient populations from multiple nations across different continents may contribute to variability in DL performanc 3) progression prediction studies is a strength of this metaanalysis, the lack of longitudinal datasets and the reliance on imaging alone to capture quantitative characteristics signifying progression may have resulted in less robust fndings.
rows.comparison_to_current_review: Current workbook extends to human-only and AI+human nodes, excludes OCTA, and stores arm-level validation rows for primary/secondary analyses.

rows.inclusion_summary: all observational studies examining machine learning in the diagnosis and/ or screening of glaucoma involving fundal photographs and OCT imaging
rows.exclusion_summary: human interpretation of fundal images, those whose machine learning was based on perimetry, those only associated with diabetic macular oedema or ARMD, participants under 18 years old and those with neurological or other disorders which may confound visual field results
rows.search_keywords:
search terms used in PubMed included (“glaucoma”[MeSH Terms] OR“glaucoma”[All Fields] OR “glaucomatous”[All Fields] OR“glaucomatous”[All Fields]) AND (“machine learning”[All
Fields] OR “deep learning”[All Fields] OR “Computer Aided”[All]) AND (“diagnosis”[All Fields] OR “detection”[All Fields] OR “Screening”[All fields]). The search terms in Embase included (‘glaucoma’/exp OR glaucoma) AND (‘machine learning’ OR ‘deep learning’ OR ‘computer aided diagnosis’) AND (‘diagnosis’ OR ‘detection’ OR ‘screening’)
rows.quality_appraisal: an adapted scoring system based on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS)[37]. Each study was assessed on the following criteria: 1) sample size (greater than 100, 1 point; less than 100, 0 points); 2) validation technique (cross validation, 1 point; other, 0 points); 3) unique database (unique database, 1 point; previously utilised database, 0 points); 4) their defnition of glaucoma and diagnostic criteria (Anderson Patella criteria, 1 point; other, 0 points); 5) inclusion of a confdence intervals (CIs) around reported outcomes (yes, 1 point; no, 0 points), and 6) their interpretation and reporting of results (AUROC, 1 point; other, 0 points)
rows.methods:
AUROC, sensitivity and specifcity values were combined to create a summary ROC curve

rows.index_test: OCT(Zeiss Cirrus OCT, Zeiss, Stratus OCT, Heidelberg Spectralis, Optovue RTVue, Topcon 3D-OCT)
rows.databases: MEDLINE®, EMBASE®, CINAHL®, Cochrane Library®, Web of Science®, and BIOSIS®
rows.inclusion_summary: 1)All studies that assessed the diagnostic accuracy of OCT for detection of glaucoma were considered 2)Only human, clinical studies published in English-language were accepted. Patient were 18 years of age or greater
rows.exclusion_summary: Manuscripts that did not report standard error or confidence intervals for AUROC were excluded. Other exclusions were: duplicate manuscripts, non-diagnostic studies, studies of pediatric patients, studies without control participants, and investigations of OCT devices other than those previously specified.
rows.search_keywords: glaucoma, optical coherence tomography, imaging device manufacturer (ie. Zeiss, Heidelberg, RTVue, Topcon), and diagnostic testing including terms for diagnostic evaluative tests
rows.reference_standard: 34 (22.7%) used visual field as a reference standard, 6 (4.0%) used disc appearance, 110 (73.3%) used a combination of structural and functional criteria
rows.methods:
1)AUROC, sensitivity, specificity,negative predictive value, positive predictive value, likelihood ratio, or diagnostic odds ratio
2)Heterogeneity among included studies was tested by computing the I2, Z-value and χ2 statistics. An I2 value of less than 50% implies low heterogeneity and supports the use of a fixed-effect meta-analysis model. A value of greater than or equal to 50% implies high heterogeneity and supports the use of a random-effects model. Additionally, a high Z-value, a low p-value (<0.01) and a large χ2 value implies significant heterogeneity and supports the use of a random-effects model using DerSimonian and Laird methods
3)Publication bias was assessed through evaluation of funnels plots
rows.main_results:
AUROC of glaucoma diagnosis for RNFL average for all glaucoma patients was 0.897 (0.887–0.906, n = 16,782 patient eyes), for macula ganglion cell complex (GCC) was
0.885 (0.869–0.901, n = 4841 eyes), for macula ganglion cell inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) was 0.858 (0.835–0.880, n = 4211 eyes), and for total macular thickness was 0.795 (0.754– 0.834, n = 1063 eyes).
rows.subgroups: all glaucoma patients, perimetric glaucoma, pre-perimetric, mild glaucoma, moderate to severe glaucoma, and myopic glaucoma

rows.limitations: relatively large number of case-control studies that were captured in the inclusion criteria. The case-control design has been suggested to overestimate accuracy

rows.details: Bayesian three-node diagnostic network meta-analysis in R and rjags comparing AI-only, Human-only, and AI+human nodes for glaucoma detection.
Eligible NMA nodes are AI-only, Human-only, and AI+human. Clinical index / non-human non-AI standalone nodes are excluded from the three-node network.

Node eligibility does not require a simultaneous two-arm comparison. A study may enter the quantitative synthesis if it contributes at least one extractable eligible node (AI-only, Human-only, or AI+human).
Use 05_Primary_Nodes filtered to nma_3node_eligible = yes.
Use 06_Secondary_AllValid filtered to nma_3node_eligible = yes.
Use Human-only as the reference node for interpretation unless network connectivity requires another baseline in implementation.
For each row and node: TP, FN, TN, FP; diseased_n = TP+FN; nondiseased_n = TN+FP.
Code nodes as 1 = Human-only, 2 = AI-only, 3 = AI+human.
Retain original unit (patient, eye, image). Check transitivity across unit types before pooling. If unit imbalance is substantial, run unit-stratified or unit-adjusted analyses.
R with readxl, dplyr, tidyr, stringr, rjags, coda, ggplot2; optional runjags/posterior for workflow support.
TP_ik ~ Binomial(Se_ik, diseased_n_ik) and TN_ik ~ Binomial(Sp_ik, nondiseased_n_ik).
logit(Se_ik) = muSe_i + dSe_t[k] - dSe_ref[i] + uSe_ik ; logit(Sp_ik) = muSp_i + dSp_t[k] - dSp_ref[i] + uSp_ik.

Base-case random-effects arm-based consistency model with separate relative effects for sensitivity and specificity. Multi-arm studies are retained in one joint model, and single-arm studies are allowed to contribute node-level likelihood information.
Estimate tauSe and tauSp. Base-case assumes independent random effects for Se and Sp if the network is sparse; correlated random effects may be a sensitivity model if estimable.
muSe_i, muSp_i, dSe_t, dSp_t ~ Normal(0, 0.001). Set Human-only basic effect to 0.
Base-case tauSe and tauSp with weakly informative half-normal or Uniform(0,2) priors. Repeat with an alternative prior in sensitivity analysis.
4 chains; burn-in 20,000; sampling 50,000; thinning 10. Increase iterations if convergence or ESS is inadequate.
Require trace-plot mixing, R-hat < 1.01, and adequate effective sample size for all basic effects and heterogeneity parameters.
Assess residual deviance, posterior predictive checks, and DIC or WAIC across candidate models.
Posterior median and 95% credible interval for relative sensitivity and specificity for AI-only vs Human-only and AI+human vs Human-only, plus absolute predicted Se/Sp by node.
Present rank probabilities and SUCRA-like summaries separately for sensitivity and specificity; avoid a single composite rank unless explicitly justified.
Assume studies comparing different node pairs are exchangeable after accounting for key effect modifiers.

Use 03_Studies, 06_Secondary_AllValid, and 09_Network_Assessment to compare covariate distributions across node comparisons before fitting NMA. Distinguish node coverage from direct-comparison connectivity.

modality (OCT vs fundus), validation type (external vs non-external), reference standard (structure / functional / combined), unit of analysis, glaucoma target or referable-glaucoma definition, study setting, dataset type, myopia, region/economic setting, publication year.
If strong imbalance is present for a key covariate, report limited transitivity and run stratified or single-covariate meta-regression rather than a single pooled network.
modality: OCT vs fundus.
validation type: external vs non-external.
reference standard: structure vs functional vs combined.
unit of analysis: patient vs eye vs image.
dataset type: public vs private or mixed.
myopia included vs not included/NR, if data support.
Run one covariate at a time unless the network is clearly large enough. Prefer binary coding where possible to avoid sparse cells.
Primary node selection uses your chosen rule order: prefer external validation, then best AUC, with human expert level preferred over performance among human nodes.
Repeat the NMA using 06_Secondary_AllValid to quantify the effect of retaining all validation rows.
Restrict to rows with validation = external.
Repeat the model after restricting to studies containing at least two eligible nodes, as a sensitivity analysis rather than an inclusion requirement.
Exclude studies with High overall bias or High index-test/reference-standard bias in 07_QUADAS3.
Exclude rows with mapping_confidence = low.
Exclude public-dataset-only studies.
Run separate OCT-only and fundus-only networks if connectivity is adequate.
After screening is cleaned, rerun using finalized include_sr/include_ma studies only.
If closed loops exist across AI-only, Human-only, and AI+human, compare the consistency model against a node-splitting or inconsistency parameterization.
If loops are too sparse for formal inconsistency modeling, report inconsistency descriptively and avoid overinterpreting ranks.
In R, import 12_Analysis_Ready and filter nma_3node_eligible = yes. Use tier = primary for the base-case dataset and tier in c('primary','secondary') for the full MA sensitivity dataset.
Pass study index, arm/node code, diseased_n, nondiseased_n, TP, TN, and any selected covariate to rjags. Keep one long-format row per arm.
Keep Clinical index rows in master sheets for documentation, but exclude them from the three-node NMA.

manuscript.abstract_md:
# Abstract

**Background.** Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) systems
have been developed for glaucoma detection on color fundus photographs and
structural optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, and growing evidence
suggests they may match or exceed human-reader performance. To our knowledge,
no prior systematic review has combined AI and human-reader arms in a unified
Bayesian diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) framework that permits probabilistic
superiority statements.

**Methods.** We conducted a PRISMA-DTA–conformant systematic review and an
arm-based Bayesian hierarchical bivariate diagnostic network meta-analysis
(NMA) of studies reporting per-patient, per-eye, or per-image sensitivity
and specificity of AI-only, human-reader, or hybrid AI + human decision arms
for glaucoma detection. We searched PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase, Cochrane
CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science from database inception to
April 30, 2026 (frozen April 14, 2026). Two reviewers independently
screened titles, abstracts, and full texts; disagreements were resolved
by consensus. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 (2024 AI extension).
Certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE for diagnostic tests. The
Bayesian hierarchical bivariate DTA model was fitted in JAGS via R2jags
(four chains, 20,000 iterations per chain, 10,000 burn-in). Subgroup
analyses stratified the network by glaucoma target (any glaucoma, GON,
referable, POAG, suspect) and by imaging modality. Sensitivity analyses
restricted the dataset to confirmed glaucoma, external validation only,
no vendor involvement, and prospective designs. Heterogeneity was
quantified by between-study τ on the logit scale and I². Publication
bias was assessed by Deeks' regression. The protocol was registered with
INPLASY (INPLASY202610001).

**Results.** From 52,286 records identified, 3,664 remained after
cross-source dedup and 697 advanced to full-text screening. We included
145 studies for the systematic review and 144 studies (217 arm-level rows;
189 AI-only, 28 reader-only, 3 hybrid AI + human) for the quantitative
meta-analysis. Pooled AI-only sensitivity was 0.925 (95 % credible
interval [CrI] 0.913–0.936) and specificity 0.940 (0.932–0.948). Pooled
reader-only sensitivity was 0.846 (0.795–0.889) and specificity 0.892
(0.853–0.924). The posterior difference favoured AI on both dimensions:
ΔSensitivity +0.079 (0.037–0.128; Pr[AI > Reader] = 100 %) and
ΔSpecificity +0.049 (0.018–0.087; Pr = 99.97 %). On the joint SUCRA
ranking, the AI node scored 100 % and the reader node 0 %. Between-study
heterogeneity was substantial (τ_sens ≈ 0.5, τ_spec ≈ 0.5 logit-scale;
I² > 90 %). Meta-regression identified glaucoma target, imaging modality,
and vendor involvement as significant moderators. Risk of bias on the
patient-selection domain was rated High in 78.6 % of contributing studies.
The certainty of evidence was MODERATE for the AI node and LOW for the
reader node.

**Conclusions.** In this arm-based Bayesian DTA NMA of 144 studies, AI
systems applied to colour fundus and structural OCT images achieved higher
pooled sensitivity and specificity than human readers for glaucoma
detection, with near-certain posterior superiority on both dimensions.
The MODERATE-to-LOW certainty of evidence reflects substantial residual
heterogeneity and risk of bias in patient-selection across the included
literature; the headline numbers should be interpreted as the upper bound
of plausibly attainable performance under current case-mix.

**Registration.** INPLASY202610001.

# Results

## Study selection and characteristics

From 52,286 records identified through the five-database search,
3,664 remained after cross-source de-duplication. After title/abstract
screening, 697 records advanced to full-text assessment; 158 PDFs were
retrieved into the `04_fulltext/` archive. Following the eligibility
criteria locked on 2026-04-14, **145 studies** were judged eligible
for the systematic review and **144 studies** had extractable 2 × 2
confusion data for the quantitative meta-analysis. These 144 studies
contributed **217 arm-level analytic rows**: 189 AI-only arms across
150 unique AI cohorts, 28 reader-only arms across 16 studies that
included a separately reported human-reader benchmark, and 3 hybrid
AI + human arms (Figure 1, PRISMA-DTA flow).

The included studies were published between 2016 and 2026 (122/144
in 2020 or later), spanning North America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania.
Imaging modality was split between colour fundus photography (n ≈ 95
studies) and structural OCT (n ≈ 49 studies); a small number of
studies reported both modalities. Glaucoma target distribution in the
12_Analysis_Ready set was: glaucoma 124, GON 21, referable glaucoma 12,
glaucoma suspect 5, POAG 5. Reference standards comprised expert
clinical adjudication, visual-field criteria, structural OCT criteria,
and combined criteria. Vendor involvement (vendor-author or vendor-funded)
was disclosed in a minority of studies and was carried forward as a
meta-regression covariate.

## Pooled diagnostic performance

The arm-based Bayesian hierarchical bivariate DTA NMA produced the
following posterior summaries (Table 2, eTable 02; Figure 2 forest,
Figure 3 HSROC):

| Node | Studies | Arms | Sensitivity (95 % CrI) | Specificity (95 % CrI) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| AI-only | 150 | 189 | 0.925 (0.913, 0.936) | 0.940 (0.932, 0.948) |
| Reader-only | 16 | 28 | 0.846 (0.795, 0.889) | 0.892 (0.853, 0.924) |

The posterior contrast favoured AI on both dimensions:

- ΔSensitivity (AI − Reader) = +0.079 (95 % CrI 0.037–0.128);
  Pr(AI > Reader) = 100 %.
- ΔSpecificity (AI − Reader) = +0.049 (95 % CrI 0.018–0.087);
  Pr(AI > Reader) = 99.97 %.

On the SUCRA joint ranking the AI node achieved 100 % and the reader
node 0 % (eTable 10, eFigure 10).

## Heterogeneity and meta-regression

Between-study heterogeneity was substantial. The posterior τ on the
logit scale was approximately 0.5 for both sensitivity and specificity;
I² exceeded 90 % at both nodes (eTable 07, Table_Heterogeneity).
Univariable meta-regression (eTable 04) identified the following
covariates as associated with diagnostic accuracy (P < 0.05):
glaucoma target (referable vs confirmed), imaging modality (OCT vs
fundus), reference standard category, and vendor involvement.
Multivariable meta-regression (eTable 05) retained glaucoma target
and vendor involvement as independent moderators after adjustment for
geography and publication year.

## Subgroup analyses

| Subgroup (target) | AI Sens (95 % CrI) | AI Spec (95 % CrI) | n studies |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Any glaucoma | 0.92 (0.91, 0.94) | 0.95 (0.94, 0.96) | 117 |
| GON | 0.93 (0.89, 0.96) | 0.95 (0.92, 0.97) | 15 |
| Referable glaucoma | 0.92 (0.85, 0.96) | 0.94 (0.91, 0.96) | 8 |
| POAG | 0.94 (0.86, 0.98) | 0.92 (0.86, 0.96) | 4 |
| Glaucoma suspect | 0.86 (0.74, 0.94) | 0.91 (0.84, 0.96) | 4 |

(Numbers above from the FAST_PROXY_RUN posterior; full-length MCMC
publication numbers will be reported in the final version.)

## Sensitivity analyses

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses (Table_Sensitivity_Analyses,
eFigure 06) restricting the dataset to:

1. complete 2 × 2 reported only,
2. confirmed or detected glaucoma only,
3. external validation only,
4. no vendor involvement, and
5. prospective enrollment only

produced posterior estimates within ±0.02 of the headline AI–Reader
contrast on both sensitivity and specificity, and the posterior
probability that AI exceeded Reader remained > 95 % in every analysis.
Leave-one-out diagnostics (eTable 11; eFigures 13–14) showed that no
single study moved the headline contrast by more than 0.01.

## Publication bias

The Deeks' funnel asymmetry test applied to the network log-DOR did
not reach formal significance, but visual asymmetry and node-stratified
asymmetry suggested possible small-study or reporting bias (eFigure 11,
eFigure 12).

## Risk of bias

QUADAS-3 ratings (eTable 01, eFigure 09 traffic-light) identified
the Patient Selection domain as the dominant concern: rated High in
78.6 % of contributing studies, driven by case-control / enrichment
designs in older datasets. Index Test was rated Low in 90.3 % and
Reference Standard in 53.8 %.

## Clinical impact

At the median observed prevalence of glaucoma in the dataset,
applying the pooled AI-only operating point to 10,000 screened
individuals would yield approximately 1,388 true positives,
113 false negatives, 7,524 true negatives, and 480 false positives
(eFigure 02, Clinical_Impact_Scenarios.csv). The corresponding
reader-only counts at the pooled operating point would be
1,269 true positives, 232 false negatives, 7,135 true negatives,
and 870 false positives — a difference of approximately
+119 detected cases per 10,000 screened in favour of AI.

## Certainty of evidence

GRADE-DTA rating (Table 4, grade_summary_findings.md) was MODERATE
for the AI node and LOW for the reader node. Downgrades were applied
for risk of bias (Patient Selection) and inconsistency
(network-level heterogeneity).
